Grand Slam Tournaments. The four most prestigious tennis competitions in the world, held annually across different continents and surfaces.

Winning all four in a single calendar year is the sport's ultimate achievement. These tournaments attract the world's best players and generate enormous commercial and cultural interest, shaping careers and legacies.

The four Grand Slams are Wimbledon on grass in England, the US Open on hard court in the United States, the French Open on clay in France, and the Australian Open on hard court in Australia. Winning all four Grand Slams in a single calendar year is called a calendar-year Grand Slam, a feat achieved only five times in modern tennis history.

The Australian Open is held in January, making it the first Grand Slam of the year. Wimbledon in summer is considered the sport's most prestigious event. Grand Slam tournaments award the most ranking points and prize money in professional tennis, making them central to player careers and the world rankings.

Rod Laver won the calendar Grand Slam twice, in 1962 and 1969. Serena Williams holds the most Grand Slam singles titles with twenty-three. Each Grand Slam has distinct characteristics. Wimbledon's grass favors fast players. The French Open clay rewards patience and spin. Hard courts are more neutral playing surfaces.

Roger Federer won a record twenty Grand Slam titles during his career, defining modern tennis excellence. Pete Sampras dominated the Grand Slams in the nineteen-nineties with sixty-four Grand Slam tournament appearances. Novak Djokovic holds the record for most Grand Slam men's singles titles with twenty-four.
